bottom_line: Tech and AI stocks just had their worst week since 2020, and the broader market has fallen into a 'correction', meaning a drop of about 10%. At the same time the Fed, the people who set interest rates, looks set to raise rates again in December because prices keep climbing. That's two hits at once: falling stock prices and more expensive borrowing.

stories.title: AI stocks got hammered
stories.real: Big tech and AI stocks sold off hard this week. Nvidia closed out its longest weekly losing streak since 2008, and Amazon slid too. Most of the market went down with them, enough to count as a 'correction', a drop of about 10%.

stories.title: The Fed is leaning toward raising rates
stories.real: Notes from the Fed's last meeting say higher rates are needed in December because people there are worried about inflation, meaning prices keep going up. Fed official Lisa Cook warned that bigger rate hikes could come. Traders put the odds of a December hike at over 90%.
stories.you: Higher rates make credit cards, car loans and mortgages cost more, but they also mean savings accounts pay a little more.

stories.title: Trump vs. the Fed on rates
stories.real: Trump says rates are too high and accuses the Fed of acting politically. He wants cuts, not hikes. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is caught between the President's pressure and the inflation problem.
stories.you: The President can push, but the Fed makes the call, so don't count on cheaper loans just because he asked for them.

stories.you: If it ever passes, people who carry a credit card balance would pay a lot less interest, but nothing has changed on your bill yet.

stories.title: Consumers and jobs still holding up
stories.real: Shoppers are still spending going into the holidays despite high prices. Slightly more people applied for unemployment aid, but the number is still low compared with the past.
stories.you: Jobs are mostly still there for now. The squeeze is in what things cost, not in layoffs.
